summary: Discusses considerations around using the IP protocol number or the payload protocol's (for example, TCP) port number to identify particular services. It is informational and examines how those fields get used as service identifiers in packet headers.

eli5.summary: Mail needs an address to reach the right person. Computers use numbers in packets to tell which service a message is for. This note thinks about the good and bad sides of that habit.

questions: how do services avoid port filtering
subtitle: Understanding how networks identify services in traffic

tldr.problem: Internet systems use port numbers and protocol fields to identify services in network traffic, and intermediate systems like firewalls often block traffic based on these identifiers. This has led to cat-and-mouse cycles where services are redesigned to avoid detection.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC examines how service identifiers work in IP headers and what happens when intermediate systems try to control traffic based on these identifiers, exploring both the usefulness of stable identifiers and the problems they create.
tldr.outcome: The IAB recommends that intermediate systems avoid taking actions based on service identifiers that would pressure applications to obscure this information, as this undermines network transparency and utility.

facts.label: Key protocol
facts.value: IP protocol numbers and TCP/UDP ports

today: RFC 3639 is an Internet Standard informational document from the Internet Architecture Board that remains relevant to network policy. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3639 is an informational document from the Internet Architecture Board that examines how service identification works in the Internet Protocol (IP) suite. It focuses on the relationship between IP protocol numbers and port numbers (which identify services like email or web traffic) and how intermediate systems—such as firewalls, routers, and network management systems—use these identifiers to make decisions about which traffic to allow or block.

The document addresses a practical tension in network design: while knowing which service a packet carries is useful for network operators, intermediate systems that block traffic based on service identifiers often encourage application developers to hide or change these identifiers to avoid filtering. This drives protocol redesign in ways that may not serve the broader Internet community.
sections.eli5: Different messages get different postal codes. Networks look at these codes to decide what to do with traffic. This note talks about whether that is a good idea.

sections.title: How Services Are Identified
sections.content:
The IP protocol suite uses several mechanisms to identify which service a packet is carrying. At the IP layer, a protocol number field indicates whether the packet contains TCP, UDP, or another upper-level protocol. When the upper-level protocol is TCP or UDP, each packet includes source and destination port numbers. These port numbers serve as identifiers: well-known ports like 25 for SMTP (email) or 80 for HTTP (web traffic) are registered with IANA and recognized worldwide.

However, the RFC emphasizes an important principle: port numbers are designed to be meaningful to end systems only. Intermediate systems in the path (routers, firewalls) should not assume that a packet using port 80 is actually web traffic, as end systems can negotiate different port numbers for their own purposes. Some protocols like the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) dynamically allocate port numbers during communication, making it impossible for intermediate systems to know the service without participating in the protocol itself.

End systems may also choose arbitrary port numbers by configuration or agreement, and many services use non-standard ports. For example, a web server might run on port 8080 instead of 80.
sections.eli5: Computers put a number in each message saying which service it is for. But those numbers are just hints for the receiving computer—the actual service might be different if the computers agreed to that.

sections.title: Service Filtering and Its Consequences
sections.content:
Many network operators deploy filtering based on service identifiers: firewalls block port 25 (SMTP) to prevent spam, for example. The RFC points out that while this is motivated by legitimate concerns, the consequences are problematic. Services can be circumvented through several methods: tunneling one protocol inside another, proxying traffic through a collaborative external server, running on alternate ports, or implementing dynamic port negotiation to avoid using a constant port address.

The result is that service-based controls impose a cost on the network community. Rather than accepting filtering, services redesign themselves—sometimes in more complex ways—to evade it. Port 25 blocking, intended to reduce spam, also blocks legitimate outgoing email for users and forces email clients to use alternate mechanisms.

The RFC suggests that intermediate systems should only take actions on service identifiers when these actions align with the interests of the parties to the communication or are specifically agreed upon (as with RSVP resource reservation or firewall rules configured for a specific enterprise).
sections.eli5: If a mail carrier refuses to deliver mail to certain addresses, people find new ways to send letters instead of just accepting it. The blocking creates more work, not less.

sections.title: Trade-offs for Network Designers
sections.content:
The RFC observes a fundamental tension in network design. Stable and visible service identifiers are useful: they allow network operators to understand traffic patterns, determine network loading, and implement helpful filtering (such as blocking DDoS attacks). However, stable identifiers also make it easy to block services, which encourages application designers to add complexity in the form of dynamic port negotiation or encryption that obscures the service.

The IAB's position is that the general interests of the Internet community are better served by transparency in service identification, and that control mechanisms should not rely on intermediate systems taking actions based on assumed relationships between port numbers and actual services. This does not oppose encryption for security or privacy, only the pressure that comes from blocking based on service identifiers.
sections.eli5: Networks work better when everyone can see what type of message is being sent. But if networks block based on what they see, services get designed to hide it.
